overview.title: Trade Journal — Overview
overview.subtitle: Why keeping a trading journal matters, and how the journal workflow fits together
overview.why_body: A trade journal is a structured record of every trade you take — your plan, your entry and exit, position size, and the reasoning and emotions behind each decision. Markets are noisy and human memory is unreliable, so without a written record it is almost impossible to tell genuine skill from luck, or to notice the recurring patterns in your own behaviour. Journaling turns scattered trades into data you can actually learn from — it transforms trading from gambling into a repeatable, measurable, and continuously improvable process.
benefits: Learn from mistakes — spot recurring errors (chasing price, oversizing, cutting winners too early) before they cost you again.
Separate skill from luck — judge each decision by the quality of your process, not just by whether the trade happened to make money.
Enforce discipline — a pre-trade plan plus an honest post-trade review reduces impulsive, emotion-driven trades.
Measure what actually works — see which setups, timeframes and market conditions truly generate your profits.
Build consistency — a repeatable plan → execute → review loop compounds small improvements over time.
Manage risk & emotions — tracking position sizing and how you felt exposes risk creep and tilt early.
overview.loop_note: Continuous-improvement loop — each review sharpens your next plan

chart_decomp.page_subtitle: Analyse price series across multiple frequencies — MODWT, EMD, VMD, CWT, Hurst, HAR

overview.hero_title: Read price the way the market actually moves
overview.hero_subtitle: A raw price line blends every force acting on a stock into a single wiggle. This workspace pulls that line apart into the layers that drive it — the slow trend, the medium cycles and the fast noise — then measures, forecasts and pattern-matches each one.
overview.goal_body: Turn one noisy price line into a set of clear, separate signals you can actually act on: know which timescale is driving the move, whether the stock is trending or mean-reverting, how risky tomorrow is, and whether a real chart pattern is forming — with guardrails so noise is not mistaken for signal.
overview.pipeline_hint: Hover any stage to see what it does and why it helps

decomp.title: Signal Decomposition
decomp.desc: Separates the price series into a smooth trend (approximation) and several oscillating components (details) using MODWT, EMD, EEMD or VMD. Each component captures movement at a different speed — long swings versus fast chatter.
decomp.benefit: See which timescale is really driving the move, and denoise the series before you model it.

time_freq.title: Time-Frequency
time_freq.desc: Maps how the strength of each frequency changes over time with the CWT scalogram and the Hilbert-Huang spectrum. Bright bands show which rhythms dominate at each date; the cone of influence marks where edge effects make readings unreliable.
time_freq.benefit: Spot regime changes — when a slow trend gives way to fast, choppy trading.

hurst.title: Hurst & Coherence
hurst.desc: Estimates the Hurst exponent on returns to tell whether the series trends (H>0.5), mean-reverts (H<0.5) or is essentially random (H≈0.5). Wavelet coherence measures how strongly two series move together across scales.
hurst.benefit: Pick the right playbook — momentum versus reversion — and uncover lead-lag links between stocks.

forecast.title: Volatility Forecast
forecast.desc: Forecasts realised volatility with the HAR model and a VMD-HAR variant, always reported next to the HAR benchmark with RMSE, MAE, R² and QLIKE so an 'improvement' has to earn it.
forecast.benefit: Size positions and set stops to expected risk, not to yesterday's calm or panic.

patterns.title: Pattern Detection
patterns.desc: Detects swing pivots and classical chart patterns across multiple scales, with a random-walk null check on the false-positive rate so random noise is not labelled as a pattern.
patterns.benefit: Surface meaningful structure — trends, reversals, nested formations — without eyeballing every chart.

benefits: Separate genuine trend from short-term noise
See which timescale is driving the current move
Know whether to trade momentum or mean-reversion
Forecast risk and size positions accordingly
Detect chart patterns objectively, with a false-positive guardrail

vol_forecast.page_subtitle: Rolling Parkinson realized variance · HAR vs VMD-HAR comparison · Diebold-Mariano test · Vol-targeting backtest with transaction costs

intro.title: Volatility Forecast & Backtest — what this is
intro.lede: Forecast how much a Vietnamese stock is likely to move tomorrow, check whether an advanced model beats a simple benchmark, and backtest whether that forecast would have improved a risk-managed strategy.
intro.def_body: Volatility is the size of a stock's price swings — high volatility means large, risky moves; low volatility means calm trading. This tool measures realized volatility from daily price data using a rolling Parkinson high–low estimator (which reads the day's high-to-low range, far less noisy than a single close-to-close return), then forecasts the next day's volatility with two models: HAR — the Heterogeneous AutoRegressive model, a standard volatility benchmark that blends daily, weekly and monthly averages — and VMD-HAR, the same model fed signals from Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD), which splits the series into smooth frequency components first.
intro.goal_title: Goal — what it does for you
intro.goal_body: Volatility drives risk and how big a position you can safely hold. Knowing tomorrow's likely volatility lets you (1) size positions to a target risk level, (2) judge — with statistics, not eyeballing — whether the more complex VMD-HAR model actually beats the simple HAR benchmark out-of-sample, and (3) see, through a realistic backtest that charges trading costs, whether acting on the forecast would have improved net return and drawdown versus simply buying and holding.
how_steps: Load data: on the ‘Forecast & Backtest’ tab, enter a ticker (e.g. VCB) and a period, then click Load. Real historical open/high/low/close prices are fetched from the market database (the green Demo button uses synthetic data instead).
Set the realized-variance window: choose the rolling window (in days) for the Parkinson estimator — a smaller window reacts faster but is noisier; a larger window is smoother (5 ≈ one trading week).
Tune the models (optional): adjust HAR and VMD-HAR parameters, or leave the sensible defaults; open Advanced params for finer control.

Run the comparison: the tool walks forward out-of-sample and reports RMSE, MAE, R² and QLIKE for both models plus a Diebold-Mariano significance test. A model only ‘wins’ if it beats the benchmark with statistical significance.
Read the chart: the actual log realized variance is on the left axis (it is naturally spiky); the HAR and VMD-HAR forecasts are on the right axis (smooth, tracking the trend).
Backtest: run the volatility-targeting backtest to scale exposure by the forecast, with transaction costs, and compare net P&L, drawdown and turnover against buy-and-hold.

event_reaction.title: Event Reaction
event_reaction.subtitle: How prices react to the surprise of discrete events — markets price the surprise, not the event.

overview.hero_title: Trade the surprise, not the headline
overview.hero_subtitle: This screen measures how a stock’s price reacts to the surprise in an event — the part the market did not already expect — and how systematically your portfolio is exposed to it.
benefits: Measure how a stock reacts to the SURPRISE in an event (earnings, rate decision, macro release) — not the headline itself. Markets price what they did not already expect.
Strip out the market-wide move (β × market) so you see the stock’s genuine abnormal return (CAR), not just “everything went up today”.
Tell a real price jump from ordinary volatility with the Lee–Mykland jump test, and calibrate its false-positive rate.
Quantify your portfolio’s exposure to surprises (γ₁): how systematically your names move per unit of surprise, with clustering-robust inference for same-day events.
No look-ahead bias: only the observed surprise and the post-event window are used — nothing from the future leaks in.

steps.title: Measure an event
steps.desc: On the Analysis tab, fill in Symbol, Market index, Event kind, Event date, Actual and Consensus, then click Measure. Surprise = Actual − Consensus.

steps.title: Read the latest measurement
steps.desc: The result card shows Surprise (σ, standardized), CAR (abnormal return), Beta, and whether the reaction was a Jump. Green = positive, red = negative.

steps.title: Build up at least 3 events
steps.desc: Each measurement is appended to the “Measured events” table. Measure several events (same or different symbols) to form a cross-section.

steps.title: Run cross-sectional exposure
steps.desc: Pick an Inference mode (cluster by event date / portfolio / iid), then click Run exposure. Read γ₁ (exposure), its t-stat, and R².

steps.title: Optional: calibrate the jump test
steps.desc: Tick “Compute jump null-FPR” before measuring to estimate the jump test’s false-positive rate under a no-jump null.

glossary.desc: Standardized surprise: how many standard deviations Actual beat/missed Consensus.
Cumulative Abnormal Return over the event window, after removing the market move.
Lee–Mykland test flag: was the move a genuine discontinuity, not normal noise?
Slope of CAR on surprise across events — the systematic reaction per unit of surprise.

event_reaction.no_rows: Measure an event to add it to the report.
event_reaction.exposure_hint: Regress CAR on the surprise across the measured events (never on the raw event). Clustering-robust handles same-day events.
